CHAPTER XI. THE EVIL WOOD

I fell fast asleep, and when I woke the sun was rising. I went to the
top again, and looked back: the hollow I had crossed in the moonlight
lay without sign of life. Could it be that the calm expanse before me
swarmed with creatures of devouring greed?

I turned and looked over the land through which my way must lie. It
seemed a wide desert, with a patch of a different colour in the
distance that might be a forest. Sign of presence, human or animal, was
none--smoke or dust or shadow of cultivation. Not a cloud floated in
the clear heaven; no thinnest haze curtained any segment of its circling
rim.

I descended, and set out for the imaginable forest: something alive
might be there; on this side of it could not well be anything!

When I reached the plain, I found it, as far as my sight could go, of
rock, here flat and channeled, there humped and pinnacled--evidently the
wide bed of a vanished river, scored by innumerable water-runs, without
a trace of moisture in them. Some of the channels bore a dry moss, and
some of the rocks a few lichens almost as hard as themselves. The air,
once “filled with pleasant noise of waters,” was silent as death.
It took me the whole day to reach the patch,--which I found indeed a
forest--but not a rudiment of brook or runnel had I crossed! Yet through
the glowing noon I seemed haunted by an aural mirage, hearing so plainly
the voice of many waters that I could hardly believe the opposing
testimony of my eyes.

The sun was approaching the horizon when I left the river-bed, and
entered the forest. Sunk below the tree-tops, and sending his rays
between their pillar-like boles, he revealed a world of blessed shadows
waiting to receive me. I had expected a pine-wood, but here were trees
of many sorts, some with strong resemblances to trees I knew, others
with marvellous differences from any I had ever seen. I threw myself
beneath the boughs of what seemed a eucalyptus in blossom: its flowers
had a hard calyx much resembling a skull, the top of which rose like a
lid to let the froth-like bloom-brain overfoam its cup. From beneath
the shadow of its falchion-leaves my eyes went wandering into deep after
deep of the forest.

Soon, however, its doors and windows began to close, shutting up aisle
and corridor and roomier glade. The night was about me, and instant
and sharp the cold. Again what a night I found it! How shall I make my
reader share with me its wild ghostiness?

The tree under which I lay rose high before it branched, but the boughs
of it bent so low that they seemed ready to shut me in as I leaned
against the smooth stem, and let my eyes wander through the brief
twilight of the vanishing forest. Presently, to my listless roving
gaze, the varied outlines of the clumpy foliage began to assume or
imitate--say rather SUGGEST other shapes than their own. A light wind
began to blow; it set the boughs of a neighbour tree rocking, and all
their branches aswing, every twig and every leaf blending its individual
motion with the sway of its branch and the rock of its bough. Among
its leafy shapes was a pack of wolves that struggled to break from
a wizard’s leash: greyhounds would not have strained so savagely! I
watched them with an interest that grew as the wind gathered force, and
their motions life.

Another mass of foliage, larger and more compact, presented my fancy
with a group of horses’ heads and forequarters projecting caparisoned
from their stalls. Their necks kept moving up and down, with an
impatience that augmented as the growing wind broke their vertical
rhythm with a wilder swaying from side to side. What heads they were!
how gaunt, how strange!--several of them bare skulls--one with the skin
tight on its bones! One had lost the under jaw and hung low, looking
unutterably weary--but now and then hove high as if to ease the bit.
Above them, at the end of a branch, floated erect the form of a woman,
waving her arms in imperious gesture. The definiteness of these and
other leaf masses first surprised and then discomposed me: what if they
should overpower my brain with seeming reality? But the twilight became
darkness; the wind ceased; every shape was shut up in the night; I fell
asleep.

It was still dark when I began to be aware of a far-off, confused,
rushing noise, mingled with faint cries. It grew and grew until a tumult
as of gathering multitudes filled the wood. On all sides at once
the sounds drew nearer; the spot where I lay seemed the centre of a
commotion that extended throughout the forest. I scarce moved hand or
foot lest I should betray my presence to hostile things.

The moon at length approached the forest, and came slowly into it: with
her first gleam the noises increased to a deafening uproar, and I began
to see dim shapes about me. As she ascended and grew brighter, the
noises became yet louder, and the shapes clearer. A furious battle was
raging around me. Wild cries and roars of rage, shock of onset, struggle
prolonged, all mingled with words articulate, surged in my ears. Curses
and credos, snarls and sneers, laughter and mockery, sacred names and
howls of hate, came huddling in chaotic interpenetration. Skeletons and
phantoms fought in maddest confusion. Swords swept through the phantoms:
they only shivered. Maces crashed on the skeletons, shattering them
hideously: not one fell or ceased to fight, so long as a single joint
held two bones together. Bones of men and horses lay scattered and
heaped; grinding and crunching them under foot fought the skeletons.
Everywhere charged the bone-gaunt white steeds; everywhere on foot or
on wind-blown misty battle-horses, raged and ravened and raved the
indestructible spectres; weapons and hoofs clashed and crushed; while
skeleton jaws and phantom-throats swelled the deafening tumult with the
war-cry of every opinion, bad or good, that had bred strife, injustice,
cruelty in any world. The holiest words went with the most hating blow.
Lie-distorted truths flew hurtling in the wind of javelins and bones.
Every moment some one would turn against his comrades, and fight more
wildly than before, THE TRUTH! THE TRUTH! still his cry. One I noted who
wheeled ever in a circle, and smote on all sides. Wearied out, a pair
would sit for a minute side by side, then rise and renew the fierce
combat. None stooped to comfort the fallen, or stepped wide to spare
him.

The moon shone till the sun rose, and all the night long I had glimpses
of a woman moving at her will above the strife-tormented multitude, now
on this front now on that, one outstretched arm urging the fight, the
other pressed against her side. “Ye are men: slay one another!” she
shouted. I saw her dead eyes and her dark spot, and recalled what I had
seen the night before.

Such was the battle of the dead, which I saw and heard as I lay under
the tree.

Just before sunrise, a breeze went through the forest, and a voice
cried, “Let the dead bury their dead!” At the word the contending
thousands dropped noiseless, and when the sun looked in, he saw never a
bone, but here and there a withered branch.

I rose and resumed my journey, through as quiet a wood as ever grew out
of the quiet earth. For the wind of the morning had ceased when the sun
appeared, and the trees were silent. Not a bird sang, not a squirrel,
mouse, or weasel showed itself, not a belated moth flew athwart my path.
But as I went I kept watch over myself, nor dared let my eyes rest on
any forest-shape. All the time I seemed to hear faint sounds of mattock
and spade and hurtling bones: any moment my eyes might open on things I
would not see! Daylight prudence muttered that perhaps, to appear, ten
thousand phantoms awaited only my consenting fancy.

In the middle of the afternoon I came out of the wood--to find before
me a second net of dry water-courses. I thought at first that I had
wandered from my attempted line, and reversed my direction; but I soon
saw it was not so, and concluded presently that I had come to another
branch of the same river-bed. I began at once to cross it, and was in
the bottom of a wide channel when the sun set.

I sat down to await the moon, and growing sleepy, stretched myself on
the moss. The moment my head was down, I heard the sounds of rushing
streams--all sorts of sweet watery noises. The veiled melody of the
molten music sang me into a dreamless sleep, and when I woke the sun
was already up, and the wrinkled country widely visible. Covered with
shadows it lay striped and mottled like the skin of some wild animal. As
the sun rose the shadows diminished, and it seemed as if the rocks were
re-absorbing the darkness that had oozed out of them during the night.

Hitherto I had loved my Arab mare and my books more, I fear, than live
man or woman; now at length my soul was athirst for a human presence,
and I longed even after those inhabitants of this alien world whom the
raven had so vaguely described as nearest my sort. With heavy yet hoping
heart, and mind haunted by a doubt whether I was going in any direction
at all, I kept wearily travelling “north-west and by south.”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER I. OUTSIDE

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’

The door slammed with the dull, decisive thud of bureaucratic finality.

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.

What grotesque heads they were! Gaunt, strange, several appearing as mere bare skulls. One lacked its lower jaw, hanging low in an expression of unutterable weariness, yet occasionally lifting high as if easing a nonexistent bit. Hovering above them, at the terminus of a branch, stood the form of a woman, waving her arms in an imperious command. The sudden definiteness of these illusions startled me, followed quickly by unease: what if they overwhelmed my sanity with deceptive reality?

Then, the twilight dissolved into absolute darkness. The wind died, sealing every shape within the void. I slept.

When consciousness returned, I was aware of a distant, confused rushing noise, mingled with faint cries. The sound grew, swelling into a tumult akin to gathering multitudes filling the wood. Simultaneously, from all directions, the noises drew nearer; the spot where I lay felt like the epicenter of a commotion extending throughout the entire forest. I barely moved a muscle, terrified of betraying my presence to hostile entities.

Finally, the moon approached the forest edge and spilled slowly into the canopy. With her first gleam, the noises escalated to a deafening uproar, and dim shapes emerged. As she ascended, brightening the gloom, the cacophony intensified and the figures clarified. A furious battle raged around me. Wild cries, roars of rage, the shock of impact, and prolonged struggles merged with articulate speech, surging in my ears. Curses and creeds, snarls and sneers, laughter and mockery, sacred names and howls of hate collided in a chaotic interpenetration.

Skeletons and phantoms fought in mad confusion. Swords swept through the phantoms, causing them only to shiver. Maces crashed onto skeletons, shattering them hideously; yet not one fell or ceased fighting so long as a single joint held two bones together. Bones of men and horses lay scattered and heaped, ground and crushed underfoot by the combatants. Everywhere, bone-gaunt white steeds charged; everywhere, on foot or mounted on wind-blown mist-horses, raged and ravened the indestructible spectres. Weapons and hooves clashed and crushed, while skeleton jaws and phantom throats swelled the deafening tumult with the war-cry of every opinion, good or evil, that had ever bred strife, injustice, or cruelty in any world.

Even the holiest words accompanied the most hateful blows. Distorted truths flew hurtling through the wind of javelins and bones. Moment by moment, allies would turn against comrades, fighting more wildly than before, screaming, "THE TRUTH!" One figure I noted wheeled endlessly in a circle, striking outward on all sides. Exhausted pairs would sit side by side for a minute, then rise to renew the fierce combat. No one stooped to comfort the fallen, nor stepped aside to spare him.

The moon shone until the sun rose, and all night long I witnessed glimpses of a woman moving at will above the strife-tormented multitude, shifting fronts, one arm urging the fight, the other pressed against her side. "Ye are men: slay one another!" she shouted. I saw her dead eyes and the dark spot upon her brow, recalling the vision from the previous night. This was the battle of the dead, which I observed and heard while lying beneath the tree.

Just before sunrise, a breeze swept through the forest, carrying a voice that cried, "Let the dead bury their dead!" At the command, the contending thousands dropped silently. When the sun peered in, it found no bone, but only here and there a withered branch.

I rose and resumed my journey through a wood as quiet as any grown from peaceful earth. The morning wind had ceased with the appearance of the sun, and the trees were silent. No bird sang, no squirrel, mouse, or weasel showed itself, and not a belated moth fluttered across my path. Yet, I maintained a vigilant watch over myself, daring not to let my eyes rest on any forest shape. Throughout the trek, faint sounds of mattocks, spades, and hurling bones echoed in my mind; any moment, my eyes might open to reveal horrors I would not wish to see. Prudence whispered that perhaps ten thousand phantoms waited only for my consenting fancy to manifest them.

By mid-afternoon, I emerged from the wood to find myself facing a second network of dry watercourses. Initially, I feared I had strayed from my intended line and reversed direction, but I soon realized otherwise, concluding I had simply reached another branch of the same ancient riverbed. I immediately began crossing it, finding myself in the bottom of a wide channel just as the sun set.

I sat to await the moon, and as drowsiness claimed me, I stretched upon the moss. The instant my head touched the ground, I heard the sounds of rushing streams—all manner of sweet, watery noises. The veiled melody of this molten music lured me into a dreamless sleep. When I awoke, the sun was already high, casting the wrinkled countryside into wide visibility. Covered in shadows, the land lay striped and mottled like the skin of a wild beast. As the sun climbed higher, the shadows diminished, as if the rocks were re-absorbing the darkness that had seeped forth during the night.

Hitherto, I had valued my Arab mare and my books more than any living man or woman. Now, at last, my soul thirsted for human presence, longing even for those inhabitants of this alien world whom the raven had vaguely described as closest to my own kind. With a heavy yet hopeful heart, my mind haunted by doubts regarding my direction, I continued wearily traveling "north-west and by south."
